name: dcled
desc: Linux driver for dream cheeky USB message board
why: A driver for an obscure USB LED message board, charming as a relic of USB poking but niche and dated.

brief.what_it_is: dcled is a Linux userland driver for the Dream Cheeky USB LED Message Board, a small scrolling LED display that was originally sold for Windows only. It works like cat: given a list of files, it sends each one to the board. With no file names it reads stdin, so it can sit at the end of a pipe. A --message option sends a single line. Version 2.2 also runs on Mac OS X and anywhere libusb can be compiled.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wanted a cool Christmas present for his brother and found the board only worked on Windows. Dream Cheeky's Hardware Developer Manual was available, so he wrote a Linux driver for fun, starting with a version that took about twelve hours on a Saturday afternoon.
brief.how_it_works: dcled is a userland program that talks to the board directly over USB through libusb 1.0, so it needs no kernel changes. Version 2.1 dropped the libhid dependency for direct libusb use. Its preamble mode shows an eye-catching graphic before scrolling text, which keeps the first words from scrolling off-screen unseen. The preamble graphic reappears whenever the screen has been idle for ten seconds, which suits monitoring a log with tail -f.

commands_seen.context: The usage line from the homepage. Options include -b brightness (0-2), -c and -C clocks, -e echo to stdout, -p preamble graphic, -r repeat forever, -s speed in ms, -t test pattern, -g font, -G font directory, -m single-line message, -n skip the device, -f fastprint, -d debug.
The author's example. It follows a log file and pipes it into dcled with preamble mode 2 (static) and echo on, so log lines also print to the terminal.

brief.install_notes: You need the libusb-1.0-dev package installed to build it. Version 2.1 removed the libhid requirement, which the author says makes builds on Debian-based systems easier. No accounts or special hardware setup are mentioned beyond the board itself. The page gives no install command or build steps.
brief.standout: The author built it in an afternoon from a manufacturer's hardware manual, and it is designed to be a cat-like pipe target. Its preamble graphics (dots, static, spiral, fire, clocks) grab attention before log text scrolls, and tachometer mode turns the display into a scriptable gauge. The homepage also mentions a cpuload helper that shows system load on the board.
brief.status: Quiet. The latest release is dcled 2.2 on Sat Feb 8 2014. The page's copyright is 2012 and nothing newer appears on it. The page gives no repository link, so I could not check commit activity.
brief.caveats: The hardware is obscure and the project is dated. The page offers no download link, only the statement that you can download version 2.2. Options and fonts are described only as the author's own list. The page mentions the Mac OS X 10.5.6 test but does not say which platforms are currently verified. The Inland Six badge is not supported by this driver, and the author said porting was not possible. The Ruby driver by Lewis Clayton is mentioned but its link was not given on the page.
quotes: Ok, so it has a silly name,  but it is a cute little scrolling led display none the less.
I set up dcled so that it works like cat.
Version 1.0 took a long saturday afternoon to write- about twelve hours.
Let me know if you find it useful!
